Senses.PreferredTarget: one’s own words from one’s own mouth
Senses.Note: Four separate interviews across two independent masters use the phrase as a verdict on an immediately spoken statement.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「如何是一言道盡底句？」師云：「親言出親口。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J10/J10nA158.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun. Miyun Yuanwu answers a question about a single phrase that says everything with ‘one’s own words from one’s own mouth.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「如何是佛法的的大意？」師云：「親言出親口。」云：「黃檗打臨濟，意旨如何？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J10/J10nA158.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun. Miyun Yuanwu gives the phrase as his answer to a question asking the exact great meaning of the teaching.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「恁麼則光前耀後去也。」師云：「親言出親口。」進云：「謝和尚。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. Feiyin Tongrong answers the layman’s conclusion with ‘one’s own words from one’s own mouth.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「者老漢話墮也。」師云：「親言出親口。」峰便喝，師云：「學來底一般。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. Feiyin Tongrong returns the phrase when Feng declares that the old man has fallen into words.

Senses.Explanation: One’s own words from one’s own mouth marks a statement as that same person’s direct, firsthand saying. In Chan interviews it is itself returned as an answer or as a compact certification of what the other person has just said. Miyun gives it as the whole answer to two different questions; Feiyin applies it first to a layman’s conclusion and then to Feng’s charge that Feiyin has fallen into words.
